points.answer: Makes bile (stored in the gall bladder and released into the duodenum)

questions.stem: Read the article and answer the questions that follow. 'Helicobacter pylori and peptic ulcers: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is a species of bacteria that has evolved to survive in the acidic environment of the stomach. It weakens the mucus lining allowing acid to damage the stomach wall, causing painful disorders such as peptic ulcers. Long term infection by H. pylori can inhibit genes that regulate normal cell division of epithelial cells in the stomach leading to cancer.' (Adapted from mayoclinic.org)

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Draw a labelled diagram of the human digestive system.

points.answer: Diagram: continuous tube from mouth to anus with stomach + small and large intestine + at least one associated gland
Labels (any correct, e.g.): mouth, oesophagus, stomach, liver, gall bladder, pancreas, small intestine (duodenum, ileum), large intestine (colon), rectum, anus

parts.scheme_note: No official scheme. Based on the 2015 Q11(b) scheme style (diagram: continuous tube + stomach + intestines + a gland; then marks for correct labels).

questions.why: Q7(d) (enzymes as selective catalysts / induced-fit model, set in the context of digestion) is a general enzyme question and is not included.

not_covered: Ingestion as a term, and the full sequence ingestion -> digestion -> absorption -> egestion (digestion and egestion are asked; ingestion and absorption are never defined) [2.6.4]
Role of each type of tooth (incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars grind) in mechanical breakdown - only the dental formula and a carnivore comparison were asked (2015) [2.6.4]
Churning in the stomach as mechanical breakdown (appears only as an accepted answer in 2008 and 2011) [2.6.4]

Modelling the complete digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats from mouth to small intestine: enzyme, production site, site of action, pH and products for each in one sequence - only asked piecemeal [2.6.4]

Explaining deamination (excess amino acids lose their amino group in the liver, which forms urea; the rest is used for energy) - only 'where urea is made' (2020) and as an accepted liver function [2.6.5]
Fate of absorbed glucose: carried in the hepatic portal vein to the liver and stored as glycogen - only the glycogen storage site in a respiration question (2018) and as accepted answers [2.6.5]
Formation of faeces and their elimination through the rectum and anus (rectum only as a diagram label; the anus never asked) [2.6.5]
Balanced diet related to health, age, gender and activity level, variety of foods and enough water - only a one-line definition (2015) [2.6.6]
Biological implications of dietary choices, e.g. high-sugar/fat/salt diets, obesity, type 2 diabetes, vegetarian/vegan diets - only 'effect of diet on the circulatory system' (2009, 2026) [2.6.6]
